title: Are they just delegating? Cross-Sample Predictions on University Students' & Teachers' Use of AI.
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether university teachers and students differ in how often they use generative AI for academic work, how much they delegate tasks to it, and how accurately they predict the other group’s AI use. The authors frame the study as a trust problem in higher education: if teachers and students misjudge each other’s AI practices, this may undermine confidence, assessment, and communication.

The study used online surveys with German university teachers and students. Participants reported their own AI use across six overlapping academic tasks: information research, literature research, writing, coding, translating, and visualizing. They also made incentivized predictions about the other group’s use and delegation levels on the same tasks. No intervention was delivered; the work is a comparative survey study with cross-sample prediction measures.

Results showed that students reported higher AI use and greater delegation than teachers on most tasks, although teachers reported more use for translation. Both groups substantially overestimated the other group’s AI use, and neither group was clearly more accurate overall. The authors conclude that there is a meaningful perception gap between teachers and students, and they argue that open discussion and transparency about AI practices are needed to support trust and equitable use of AI in higher education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI / AI chatbot tools used for academic tasks such as information research, writing, programming, translating, and visualizing; the paper does not identify a specific product in the main study measures.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers and students self-reported frequency of use and degree of delegation to AI across overlapping academic tasks, and predicted the other group’s use and delegation.

findings.finding_summary: This was a survey study of university teachers (n=113) and students (n=123) in which participants reported their own AI use and delegation across academic tasks and made cross-sample predictions. Students reported higher frequency of AI use than teachers for five of six tasks (overall b=-0.35, d=0.36), and higher delegation (overall b=-15.72, d=0.66); teachers reported higher use for translation only.
findings.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use and self-reported degree of AI delegation across six overlapping academic tasks

quality_tier_rationale: This is a correlational survey study with self-reports and cross-sample predictions, not an experiment or intervention. It provides useful descriptive evidence about AI use patterns but does not test a coaching system or causal effect on teacher practice.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported group differences are modest to medium in size, with d=0.36 for frequency and d=0.66 for delegation. However, the paper is about general AI use perceptions rather than interactive coaching, so direct instructional impact is limited.
